page: Amazon Web Services c7i.metal-48xl is a bare-metal, compute-optimized server instance powered by dedicated Intel Xeon 8488C processors. Utilizing the x86_64 architecture, it features 192 vCPUs across 96 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, operating at a base clock speed of 3.2 GHz. The processor configuration includes a 105 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for tile and int8 operations. The system is equipped with 384.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory running at 5 GHz, providing a resource density of 2.0 GB of RAM per physical core. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPUs, relying instead on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 50 Gbps.

Benchmark data highlights the server's multi-core processing capabilities, with stress-ng multi-core performance and PassMark CPU scores placing it in the top tier. The DDR5 memory subsystem delivers top-tier read-only bandwidth, reaching 13,985.92 GB/sec for cached small blocks and 423.72 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. The presence of Intel AMX and AVX-512 instructions translates to top-tier performance in PassMark extended instructions, encryption, and physics tests. In real-world application simulations, the instance achieves top-tier throughput in software compilation, ray tracing, text processing, and Redis SET operations, which registers at 191.08 million operations per second. It also demonstrates strong performance in large language model inference, processing 41.42 tokens per second for prompt processing on a 70B model.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the c7i.metal-48xl offers high compute density and memory bandwidth relative to its hardware profile, making it highly efficient for CPU-bound parallel workloads. However, the lack of bundled local storage and dedicated GPUs represents a tradeoff for workloads requiring high-speed local scratch space or hardware-accelerated graphics processing. This bare-metal instance is best suited for compute-intensive workloads, including high-performance computing, large-scale software compilation, CPU-based machine learning inference, intensive database operations, and high-throughput web serving.
